_comment: Java Interview Kit — quiz questions for chapters 2-4.
Keyed by TOPIC SLUG; scripts/java-quiz-export.js resolves slugs to topicIds.
All 'concept' type — the vm verification gate cannot execute Java (PRD-009 §5.1).

questions.prompt: What is the first statement of every Java constructor?
options: A call to this(...) or super(...) — inserted implicitly as super() if you write neither
A null check on the parameters
Nothing is required before the constructor body
The first field assignment
questions.explanation: Every constructor begins by invoking another one: this(...) to delegate within the class, or super(...) to the parent. If you write neither, the compiler inserts super(). That is why a single new runs a chain of constructors from Object downward, guaranteeing inherited state is initialised before the class's own body runs.
questions.citation: How it works — chain upward

questions.prompt: A Parent constructor calls an overridable method init(). Child overrides init() and reads its own field 'value', initialised to "ready". What does the override see?
options: A compile error — a constructor cannot call an overridable method
null, because the parent constructor runs BEFORE the child's field initialisers
The parent's version of init() runs instead, so the field is irrelevant
"ready", because field initialisers run before any constructor
questions.explanation: Dispatch is dynamic, so Child.init() runs. But initialisation order is parent instance initialisers, parent constructor body, THEN child instance initialisers — so the child's fields are still at their defaults when the override executes. This is why an overridable method must never be called from a constructor; make such methods private, static or final.
questions.citation: Code examples — the classic constructor bug

questions.prompt: You add a constructor User(String name) to a class that previously had none. What breaks?
options: Serialization only
Nothing — the compiler still provides a no-arg constructor as well
Existing calls to new User(), because the default constructor disappears once you declare any constructor
All subclasses, because constructors are inherited
questions.explanation: The compiler generates a no-arg constructor only when you declare no constructor at all. Declaring any constructor removes the free one, so previously valid new User() calls stop compiling. Constructors are also not inherited, which is a separate point.
questions.citation: How it works — the default constructor

questions.prompt: Parent p = new Child();  Which of p.label (a field), p.instanceMethod() and p.staticMethod() resolve to the Child version?
options: All three, because the object is a Child
Only the field, because fields are looked up on the instance
None — the reference type is Parent
Only p.instanceMethod() — fields and static methods are resolved from the declared type
questions.explanation: Only instance methods are dynamically dispatched. Fields and static methods are resolved at compile time from the declared type, so re-declaring either in a subclass HIDES rather than overrides it. This is a strong argument for keeping fields private and calling statics on the class.
questions.citation: Code examples — fields and static methods are not polymorphic

questions.prompt: Which change to an overriding method will NOT compile?
options: Declaring a broader checked exception than the parent declared
Declaring no checked exceptions at all
Returning Dog where the parent returned Animal
Widening access from protected to public
questions.explanation: An override may narrow or drop checked exceptions but never broaden them, because code compiled against the parent would not be prepared to handle the new one. Covariant returns and widened access are both allowed. All of these rules exist to preserve Liskov substitutability.
questions.citation: How it works — the override rules table

questions.prompt: Why is 'mark methods final for performance' obsolete advice on a modern JVM?
options: Because final methods are actually slower than virtual ones
Because the JIT devirtualises monomorphic call sites and inlines them behind a guard, deoptimising if a second type appears
Because all methods are final by default since Java 8
Because the JVM no longer uses virtual method tables
questions.explanation: Most call sites see only one receiver type in practice. The JIT observes this, compiles a direct call guarded by a class check and inlines it, falling back safely if the assumption breaks. So final should express design intent — this must not be overridden — rather than being used to chase speed.
questions.citation: Under the hood — dynamic dispatch and devirtualisation

questions.prompt: Since Java 8 gave interfaces default methods, what is the remaining fundamental difference from an abstract class?
options: Abstract classes can be instantiated directly
Interfaces cannot be used as types
Interfaces have no instance state — an abstract class can hold mutable per-object fields and a constructor
Interfaces still cannot contain any method bodies
questions.explanation: Both can carry method bodies now, so the old answer is wrong. The line that still holds is state: any field declared in an interface is implicitly public static final — a shared constant, not per-object state — and interfaces have no constructor. That is also why default methods cannot read or write instance state.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — the line that still holds after Java 8

questions.prompt: Why were default methods added in Java 8?
options: To replace abstract classes entirely
To allow interfaces to hold mutable state
To make lambdas possible
To let interfaces be evolved without breaking existing implementations — adding stream() to Collection as an abstract method would have broken every List in existence
questions.explanation: Backward-compatible interface evolution was the motivating problem. Java 8 needed to add stream() and forEach() to Collection; as abstract methods that would have broken every implementation on the planet. A default gives a working body so existing code keeps compiling.
questions.citation: How it works — why default methods were added

questions.prompt: A class implements two interfaces that both declare the same default method. What happens?
options: It will not compile until the class overrides the method — it can delegate explicitly with A.super.method()
Both run, in declaration order
The JVM picks one at random at run time
The first interface in the implements clause wins
questions.explanation: Java refuses to guess: inheriting unrelated defaults for the same signature is a compile error until the class provides its own override, which may delegate with A.super.method(). Note also that a concrete method inherited from a superclass always beats an interface default.
questions.citation: How it works — conflicting defaults

questions.prompt: What is the default access level when you write no modifier?
options: protected
package-private — visible only within the same package
private
public
questions.explanation: The default is package-private, the second-narrowest level. It is genuinely useful: classes collaborating closely inside one package can cooperate without exposing anything outside it. Developers coming from C# often assume the default is public.
questions.citation: How it works — the visibility table

questions.prompt: A subclass in a different package tries to access a protected field on a Base-typed reference to another object. What happens?
options: It compiles only if the field is also final
It compiles — protected means any subclass can access it anywhere
It is a compile error: cross-package protected access works only through a reference of the subclass's own type
It compiles but throws IllegalAccessError at run time
questions.explanation: Cross-package protected access is restricted to the subclass's own inherited member, reached through a reference of that subclass type. Accessing the same member on an arbitrary Base instance is rejected — the restriction stops subclassing being used as a back door into unrelated objects.
questions.citation: How it works — the asterisk on protected

questions.prompt: A class has a private list and a getter that returns it directly. Why is that a problem?
options: It causes a memory leak
It is not a problem — the field is private, so the object is encapsulated
It prevents the class from being serialised
The caller receives a reference to the live internal collection and can clear or reorder it, bypassing every invariant the class enforces
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is about controlling state, not about the private keyword. Handing out the live collection hands out control of it — the same pass-by-value reasoning from Chapter 1. Return List.copyOf(...) for a snapshot, or an unmodifiable view.
questions.citation: Code examples — the leaky getter

questions.prompt: You override equals() but not hashCode(). You put a key in a HashMap and look it up with an equal key. What happens?
options: It returns null — the two keys produce different hash codes and map to different buckets, so equals is never even consulted
It returns the value, because equals() is what a HashMap uses
It throws IllegalStateException
It works, but the map is slower
questions.explanation: A hash lookup is two steps: hashCode picks the bucket, then equals confirms the key within it. With an inherited identity hashCode, two equal objects land in different buckets, so the search happens in the wrong place and equals is never reached. Nothing throws — the entry is in the table and unreachable.
questions.citation: Code examples — the bug, reproduced in six lines

questions.prompt: Can two objects that are NOT equal share a hash code?
options: Only if they are instances of different classes
Yes, and it is expected — a hash code is 32 bits over an unbounded object space, so collisions are inevitable
Only when hashCode() is badly implemented
No — that would violate the contract
questions.explanation: The contract runs one way only: equal objects MUST share a hash code, but unequal objects may collide. That is why a hash map always calls equals after locating the bucket. Frequent collisions are a performance concern, never a correctness one.
questions.citation: How it works — the hashCode contract

questions.prompt: Why is 'implement equals(MyType other)' a bug?
options: It breaks serialisation
It is not — that is the type-safe way to write it
It overloads Object.equals(Object) rather than overriding it, so every library that calls equals(Object) — including HashMap — ignores it
It causes infinite recursion
questions.explanation: Object declares equals(Object). A method taking a narrower parameter type is a different signature, so it is an overload — the JDK continues to call the inherited identity comparison. Writing @Override turns this silent behavioural bug into a compile error, which is why it is close to mandatory.
questions.citation: Common mistakes — writing equals(MyType o)

questions.prompt: final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();  Which operation fails to compile?
options: list.add("x")
list.clear()
list.remove(0)
list = new ArrayList<>()
questions.explanation: final fixes the binding, not the object. You cannot reassign the variable, but the ArrayList it points at remains fully mutable. Real immutability is a property of the object — List.of(...) or a record — not of the reference.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — final makes the reference immutable, not the object

questions.prompt: Creating two instances of a class whose parent and child each have a static block and an instance block — how many times does each static block run?
options: Once each, when the class is first initialised — statics do not repeat per instance
Twice each, once per instance
Once for the parent and twice for the child
It depends on the constructor used
questions.explanation: Static fields and static blocks run exactly once, when the class is first initialised, parent before child. Instance initialisers and constructor bodies run on every new: parent instance init, parent constructor, child instance init, child constructor.
questions.citation: Code examples — the order question

questions.prompt: Why is the initialisation-on-demand holder idiom a correct lazy singleton with no synchronized keyword?
options: Because static fields are volatile by default
Because the JVM guarantees a class's static initialiser runs exactly once, serialised under an internal lock, and the holder class is only initialised on first access
Because the JIT inlines the getter
It is not correct — it needs double-checked locking
questions.explanation: Class initialisation is lazy and thread-safe by specification. The nested holder class is not initialised until getInstance() first touches it, and the JVM serialises that initialisation, giving laziness and thread safety for free. The same lock is also why a blocking static initialiser can deadlock.
questions.citation: Under the hood — class initialisation is thread-safe

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the reasons String is immutable?
options: It allows the hash code to be computed once and cached
It removes a time-of-check-to-time-of-use window in security-sensitive APIs
It makes String operations faster than StringBuilder operations
It makes the string pool safe, since one object can be shared by many references
questions.explanation: Immutability actually costs performance for repeated edits — every transformation allocates a new object, which is exactly why StringBuilder exists. The four genuine reasons are security, hash caching, thread safety and pooling.
questions.citation: How it works — the four reasons

questions.prompt: Why are passwords recommended to be held in a char[] rather than a String?
options: char[] uses less memory
String cannot hold non-ASCII characters
char[] is encrypted automatically by the JVM
A char[] can be overwritten with Arrays.fill once used; an immutable String cannot be erased and may linger in the pool and in heap dumps until collected
questions.explanation: The property that makes String safe elsewhere works against you here: you cannot wipe it. A char[] can be zeroed immediately after use, which is why JPasswordField.getPassword() returns one.
questions.citation: Code examples — the security argument

questions.prompt: How much memory does a Java String use per character on Java 9 and later?
options: One byte for Latin-1 content, two for anything wider — compact strings store a byte[] plus a coder flag
Always 4 bytes, for full Unicode
It depends on the platform's default charset
Always 2 bytes — String stores a char[]
questions.explanation: Before Java 9, String stored a char[] at two bytes per character. Compact strings changed it to a byte[] with a one-byte coder, so ASCII text — the overwhelming majority — uses one byte per character. 'A Java String is 2 bytes per char' has been wrong since Java 9.
questions.citation: Under the hood — compact strings

questions.prompt: String a = "hi"; String b = new String("hi");  What are a == b and a.equals(b)?
options: true and false
false and true — b is a distinct heap object, but the characters match
true and true
false and false
questions.explanation: The literal is pooled; new String() explicitly allocates a separate object, which is essentially its only purpose. == compares identity so it is false; equals compares characters so it is true. b.intern() would return the pooled instance, which would be == to a.
questions.citation: Code examples — the four comparisons

questions.prompt: Why is "hel" + "lo" == "hello" true, but prefix + "lo" == "hello" false when prefix is a non-final variable holding "hel"?
options: It is a JVM bug fixed in Java 9
The + operator behaves differently on variables
Constant folding: javac evaluates the all-literal expression at compile time so it becomes a pooled literal, while the variable version is built on the heap at run time
Non-final variables are never pooled at all, including their contents
questions.explanation: If the compiler can evaluate the expression — both operands literals, or a final variable initialised with a constant — the result is a literal and gets pooled. With a non-final variable the concatenation happens at run time. That the answer depends on a final keyword elsewhere is the strongest argument against ever using == on strings.
questions.citation: How it works — compile-time constant folding

questions.prompt: What is the modern alternative to calling intern() to reduce memory from duplicate strings?
options: Increasing -XX:StringTableSize
Calling System.gc() more often
Storing strings as char[] instead
G1 string deduplication (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication), which merges identical strings' backing arrays during GC with no code changes
questions.explanation: intern() adds pool insertion cost and contention and requires changing application code. G1's string deduplication achieves most of the memory benefit in the collector, transparently. Increasing the string table size only helps if you are already interning heavily.
questions.citation: Under the hood — the modern alternative to intern()

questions.prompt: Why is building a string with += inside a loop O(n squared)?
options: Because each iteration allocates a new String and copies every character accumulated so far
Because string concatenation always sorts the characters
It is not — the compiler converts it to a StringBuilder automatically
Because the JVM cannot optimise loops containing string operations
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so iteration i must allocate a new object and copy all i characters so far; summed over n iterations that is quadratic copying plus n objects of garbage. A StringBuilder appends into one buffer that doubles when full, giving amortised O(n).
questions.citation: How it works — the complexity change

questions.prompt: Is it still accurate to say 'the compiler turns every + into a StringBuilder'?
options: Yes, on every Java version
It was true up to Java 8; since Java 9 a single concatenation expression compiles to invokedynamic against StringConcatFactory, which sizes the result and fills it in one pass
No — the compiler never optimises string concatenation
Only when the operands are compile-time constants
questions.explanation: Java 9 changed the strategy: an invokedynamic call site is linked at run time to a generated method, which is faster than the old builder expansion. Either way the optimisation applies to a single expression — a loop is a sequence of separate expressions each producing a complete new string, which no code generation can rescue.
questions.citation: Under the hood — the Java 9 invokedynamic change

questions.prompt: When is StringBuffer the right choice over StringBuilder?
options: Whenever the code might one day be multi-threaded
When building very large strings, because it is faster
Essentially never — per-method locking costs when unneeded and does not make a SEQUENCE of appends atomic, which is what shared use would actually require
When the builder is a field rather than a local variable
questions.explanation: StringBuffer synchronises each method, which is the wrong granularity: unnecessary for the usual case of a local builder, and insufficient for genuine sharing, where you would need the whole append sequence to be atomic. Give each thread its own builder, or collect and join.
questions.citation: How it works — why StringBuffer is obsolete

questions.prompt: Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128.  What are a == b and c == d?
options: true and true
false and false
false and true
true and false — valueOf returns a cached shared object for -128 to 127 and a new object above that
questions.explanation: Autoboxing calls Integer.valueOf, which serves values from -128 to 127 out of a preallocated cache, so both variables reference the same object. Above the range each call allocates. equals() is true in both cases, which is why it is the only correct comparison.
questions.citation: Code examples — the famous puzzle

questions.prompt: Which wrapper types does the JLS guarantee are cached?
options: Boolean, all Byte values, Character 0-127, and Short/Integer/Long from -128 to 127 — Float and Double are never cached
Only Integer, from -128 to 127
Only Boolean and Character
All of them, across their full ranges
questions.explanation: Those are the mandated ranges. Floating-point wrappers are never cached, so Double.valueOf(1.0) == Double.valueOf(1.0) is false. The Integer upper bound is also tunable with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax, which means identical code can behave differently on two JVMs — a decisive reason never to rely on ==.
questions.citation: How it works — the cached ranges

questions.prompt: List<Integer> list contains 10, 20, 30. What does list.remove(1) do?
options: Removes the value 1, leaving the list unchanged since it is not present
Removes the element at index 1, which is 20 — remove(int) and remove(Object) are overloads and an int literal selects the index version
Removes both the element at index 1 and any element equal to 1
Throws, because the argument is ambiguous
questions.explanation: Overload resolution happens at compile time on the declared argument type, so an int literal picks remove(int index). To remove by value you must box explicitly: list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)). It is Chapter 2's overload resolution biting inside the standard library.
questions.citation: Code examples — the nastier trap

questions.prompt: Why does Map not extend Collection?
options: For historical reasons only — it was an oversight in Java 1.2
Because Map is not iterable
Because a Map's unit is a key-value PAIR, so Collection's element-based contract — add(E), contains(E), iterator over E — would be meaningless or require an arbitrary choice between key and value
Because Map allows duplicate keys
questions.explanation: The abstractions genuinely do not fit. Rather than force the inheritance, Map is a separate root that offers collection VIEWS — keySet(), values() and entrySet() — when you need one.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — two independent roots

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Arrays.asList("a","b") and List.of("a","b")?
options: List.of is a view of the array; Arrays.asList is a copy
Arrays.asList is immutable; List.of is mutable
They are identical
Arrays.asList is a fixed-size mutable view backed by the array — set works and writes through, add throws — while List.of is fully immutable and rejects nulls
questions.explanation: Arrays.asList gives a fixed-size wrapper: you can replace elements and the writes go through to the backing array, but you cannot add or remove. List.of (Java 9+) is genuinely immutable and throws on any modification, and it rejects null elements.
questions.citation: Code examples — factory methods and the trap in one

questions.prompt: Why does ConcurrentHashMap reject null keys and values when HashMap allows them?
options: Because get() returning null would be ambiguous between 'absent' and 'mapped to null', and unlike a HashMap you cannot resolve it with containsKey — the state may change between the two calls
To save memory
It is an arbitrary API restriction with no technical reason
Because null cannot be hashed
questions.explanation: In a single-threaded HashMap you can disambiguate with a follow-up containsKey. Concurrently that check is worthless because another thread may act in between. Banning null makes null unambiguously mean absent, which is what makes correct concurrent code writable.
questions.citation: Under the hood — null handling by implementation

questions.prompt: LinkedList has O(1) insertion. Why is it still usually slower than ArrayList in practice?
options: Because LinkedList does not implement List properly

Because its O(1) applies only at the ends or through an iterator you already hold — and because pointer-chasing to scattered nodes misses cache while ArrayList's shift is one contiguous System.arraycopy
Because LinkedList is synchronised
Because ArrayList caches its elements in the CPU register file
questions.explanation: Positional insertion still has to walk the chain to find the position, so add(i, e) is O(n) anyway. And constants dominate at realistic sizes: contiguous memory is prefetched by the CPU, while each node hop is a potential cache miss, with about 40 bytes of overhead per element.
questions.citation: Interview lens — but LinkedList has O(1) insertion

questions.prompt: How does ArrayList grow when it runs out of capacity?
options: It converts to a LinkedList
It doubles the array on every add
It allocates a new array of roughly 1.5 times the size and copies with System.arraycopy — amortised O(1) per add
It allocates one extra slot each time
questions.explanation: Default capacity is 10, allocated lazily on the first add; growth is about 1.5x with a copy. That makes add amortised O(1) even though an individual add can be O(n). Passing an initial capacity avoids the intermediate allocations entirely.
questions.citation: How it works — ArrayList growth

questions.prompt: What does list.subList(0, 5) return?
options: A new ArrayList with the same elements
An independent copy of the first five elements
An immutable snapshot
A live VIEW onto the original list — writes go through, and structurally modifying the parent invalidates it
questions.explanation: It is a view, not a copy. That makes list.subList(a, b).clear() a neat way to delete a range, and a trap if you assumed independence. Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(...) when you want a real copy.
questions.citation: Under the hood — subList is a view

questions.prompt: Why does HashMap apply h ^ (h >>> 16) to the key's hash code?
options: Because the bucket index is computed by masking the LOW bits, so mixing the high bits down means they still influence which bucket is chosen
To make the hash code positive
To compress the hash into fewer bits
To detect collisions
questions.explanation: Since the table length is a power of two, the index is hash & (length - 1) — a mask that keeps only low bits. Without spreading, two keys differing only in their high bits would always collide. This one line rescues mediocre hashCode implementations.
questions.citation: How it works — step 2, spreading

questions.prompt: When does a HashMap bin convert from a linked list into a red-black tree?
options: Never — that is a ConcurrentHashMap feature
When the bin reaches 8 nodes AND the table is at least 64 entries long
As soon as any collision occurs
When the map exceeds its load factor
questions.explanation: Treeification, added in Java 8, needs both conditions: 8 nodes in one bin and a table of at least 64. Below that table size the map resizes instead, because spreading entries is cheaper than building a tree. It untreeifies below 6. The motivation was hash-collision denial-of-service attacks, not everyday performance.
questions.citation: How it works — treeification

questions.prompt: With the default capacity of 16 and load factor 0.75, which insertion triggers the first resize?
options: The 8th
The 16th
The 13th — the threshold is 16 x 0.75 = 12
The 12th
questions.explanation: The map resizes when size exceeds capacity times load factor, so the 13th entry triggers a doubling to 32 and rehomes everything. Because capacity is a power of two, one extra hash bit decides each entry's fate: it stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity, so Java 8 splits each bin in one pass with no rehashing.
questions.citation: How it works — resize

questions.prompt: How do you build an LRU cache from the JDK's collections?
options: Use an ArrayDeque and move entries to the front on access
Use a TreeMap sorted by last access time
Use a ConcurrentHashMap with a background eviction thread
Extend LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true in the three-arg constructor and override removeEldestEntry to return size() > capacity
questions.explanation: That is the whole implementation. Access order means every get moves the entry to the end of the internal linked list, and removeEldestEntry lets the map evict on insertion. Built from scratch it would be a HashMap plus a doubly-linked list — which is exactly what LinkedHashMap is.
questions.citation: Code examples — the LRU cache

questions.prompt: TreeMap decides whether two keys are the same using…
options: compareTo or the supplied Comparator — a result of 0 means 'same key', regardless of what equals says
equals and hashCode, like HashMap
reference identity
equals only
questions.explanation: This is how new TreeMap<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER) gives a case-insensitive map for free, and also how a comparator on a single field can silently overwrite entries equals would keep distinct. The javadoc recommends the ordering be consistent with equals for this reason.
questions.citation: How it works — TreeMap requires ordering

questions.prompt: Which map would you choose to answer 'which pricing tier applies to a spend of 88?'
options: LinkedHashMap, relying on insertion order
TreeMap, using floorEntry(88) to get the greatest key not exceeding 88 in O(log n)
Any of them — the choice makes no difference
HashMap, iterating the keys and comparing
questions.explanation: The question is a RANGE query, which is precisely what TreeMap's navigation methods exist for: floorKey, ceilingKey, headMap, subMap. Iterating a HashMap to find it is O(n) per lookup and reimplements what the data structure already provides.
questions.citation: Code examples — TreeMap navigation methods

questions.prompt: How does HashSet guarantee uniqueness?
options: It uses reference identity only
It scans the set on each add to check for duplicates
It wraps a HashMap, storing each element as a KEY with a single shared dummy value — uniqueness comes entirely from map key uniqueness, i.e. from hashCode and equals
It sorts elements and compares neighbours
questions.explanation: HashSet implements nothing itself. add returns map.put(e, PRESENT) == null, which is why it tells you whether the element was new. Everything true of HashMap keys — the equals/hashCode contract, mutable-key danger, arbitrary iteration order — is therefore true of HashSet elements.
questions.citation: The concept, simply — HashSet is a HashMap

questions.prompt: How do you deduplicate a list while preserving the original order?
options: Collections.sort followed by a manual scan
new ArrayList<>(new HashSet<>(list))
list.stream().sorted().distinct().toList()
new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)), or list.stream().distinct().toList()
questions.explanation: LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order while removing duplicates, and Stream.distinct preserves encounter order too. A plain HashSet would deduplicate but scramble the order, and sorting changes the order by definition.
questions.citation: Code examples — deduplicate keeping order

questions.prompt: There is no ConcurrentHashSet class. What do you use instead?
options: ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()
CopyOnWriteArraySet for all cases
A ConcurrentLinkedQueue with manual duplicate checks
Collections.synchronizedSet(new HashSet<>())
questions.explanation: newKeySet() returns a set backed by a ConcurrentHashMap — the same dummy-value technique applied to the concurrent implementation, so it inherits lock-free reads and per-bin write locking. Collections.newSetFromMap is the general form. synchronizedSet wraps one lock around everything and still needs manual locking around iteration.
questions.citation: Under the hood — the concurrent set

questions.prompt: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety in Java 8 and later?
options: By copying the whole table on every write
Lock-free reads via volatile fields, plus writes that CAS into an empty bin or synchronise on the bin's first node
By dividing the table into 16 segments, each with its own lock
By synchronising every method on the map object
questions.explanation: Segments were the Java 7 design and were removed in Java 8, which capped concurrency at the segment count regardless of table size. The modern implementation locks per bin, so writers to different bins never contend, and get() takes no lock at all.
questions.citation: How it works — what changed in Java 8

questions.prompt: Is 'if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)' safe on a ConcurrentHashMap?
options: Yes, as long as the map is declared final
Only if the value is immutable
No — each call is atomic but the SEQUENCE is not, so another thread can act between them. Use putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, compute or merge
Yes — ConcurrentHashMap makes all operations on it atomic
questions.explanation: Per-operation atomicity does not compose. Any read-modify-write must go through one of the atomic compound methods, which perform the whole operation under the bin's lock. This is the single most common misuse of the class.
questions.citation: How it works — what it does not give you

questions.prompt: When is CopyOnWriteArrayList the right choice?
options: For large lists that are frequently appended to
For any list accessed from multiple threads
For producer-consumer hand-off between threads
When reads vastly outnumber writes and iteration must never throw — a listener list configured at startup is the classic case
questions.explanation: Every write copies the entire backing array, so iteration is a lock-free snapshot but writes are expensive. It is ideal for read-mostly data and completely wrong for anything write-heavy. Producer-consumer wants a BlockingQueue instead.
questions.citation: Under the hood — when CopyOnWriteArrayList is wrong

questions.prompt: What mechanism produces ConcurrentModificationException?
options: A modCount counter on the collection, snapshotted by the iterator at creation and compared on every next() call
A lock timeout inside the iterator
A hash of the collection's contents, recomputed on each iteration step
The JVM detects concurrent access to the collection from two threads
questions.explanation: Every structural change increments modCount; the iterator remembers the value it saw at creation and throws if they diverge. No threads are involved — the usual cause is one thread modifying a collection inside its own loop, which is why the exception's name misleads people.
questions.citation: How it works — the mechanism

questions.prompt: Which operation during iteration will NOT trigger the fail-fast check?
options: map.remove(k)
list.set(i, x) — replacing an element is not a STRUCTURAL modification
list.add(x)
list.remove(x)
questions.explanation: Only structural changes — adding or removing elements — increment modCount. Replacing an existing element's value with set(), or a map.put on a key that already exists, leaves the structure unchanged and is safe during iteration.
questions.citation: How it works — 'structural' is the key word

questions.prompt: Should you catch ConcurrentModificationException?
options: Yes, and retry the iteration
Yes, if the collection is shared between threads

questions.explanation: The check is unsynchronised and explicitly best-effort, so it may or may not fire in a genuinely concurrent scenario. It exists to surface bugs during development. The fix is to change the loop — removeIf, an explicit Iterator with remove(), iterate a copy, or collect and remove afterwards.
